chunks: 34 - Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar said: I wrote to Abu Muhammad (peace be upon him).

Regarding a man who bought an animal from another man, and an incident occurred in it, such as removing its hoof or shoeing it, or riding it for a distance of three farsakhs; is he entitled to return it within the three days during which he has the option [of rescission] after the incident that occurred in it, or the riding that he rode it for three farsakhs?
So he (peace be upon him) wrote: 'If an incident occurs in it, then the purchase becomes binding, if God wills.'

key_terms.أَحْدَثَ فِيهَا حَدَثًا: An incident occurred in it (referring to a change or defect)
key_terms.الْخِيَار: The option (of rescission in a contract)
key_terms.فَرَاسِخَ: For three farsakhs (a unit of distance)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on returning a purchased animal if an incident occurs after the sale?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Hadi (AS) clarifies that the occurrence of a specific incident (hadath), such as shoeing or riding, does not automatically grant the buyer the right of rescission (khiyar) unless it constitutes a defect or is agreed upon. This ruling emphasizes that the sale becomes binding (thabit) upon the occurrence of the event, distinguishing between mere usage or alteration and actual defects that justify returning the animal. This highlights the Shia juristic principle that 'khiyar al-hadis' is contingent on the nature of the incident affecting the animal's value or utility, rather than being an automatic right for any post-sale modification.
